newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe bank seen favouring softer local currency.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe bank seen favouring softer local currency.

text.p: The Zimbabwe dollar's steady downward trend over the last 10 days reflects a desire by the central bank to see a softer local currency ahead of an annual national budget later this month, foreign currency analysts say.

The Zimbabwe dollar has lost some nine cents against the U.S. dollar over the period, a fall triggered by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe buying foreign currency in a market that was already buckling under import pressure.

Foreign currency dealers told Reuters that the central bank seemed happy to stand on the sidelines and watch the dollar go down, only coming in on Friday to smooth the fall when the unit shed three cents.
"I think the Reserve Bank move is monetary. They could be unhappy with an overvalued Zimbabwe dollar...," one foreign exchange dealer said.

The buying could have been linked to pressure on the government to pay off some of its foreign debt, or possibly to something in the forthcoming budget that would make a weaker Zimbabwe dollar desirable, he said.

He pointed to the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe's steadfast intervention to mop up foreign currency which kept the local unit from appreciating beyond the 11.3000/3100 level against the U.S. dollar. This was despite a steady inflow of receipts from annual tobacco auctions which opened in April.

In his first monetary policy statement for the year in March, Reserve Bank governor Leonard Tsumba said the bank expected to see an improvement in gross foreign exchange reserves over the next several months on the back of proceeds from the tobacco sales.

This would revive Zimbabwe's import cover which had dwindled to just under three months as of March from five months last September largely due to pressure from accelerated capital repayments, Tsumba said.
The Foreign Exchange Association of Zimbabwe says Zimbabwe now has enough foreign currency reserves to cover five-and-half months' imports due to the tobacco sales.
But on Tuesday import pressure was still evident in the market and the local unit closed the day at 11.4050/4150 against the U.S. currency compared to Monday's 11.3950/4050.
"If things keep going at this rate, I see the dollar hitting 11.4500/4600 by budget time (July 24)," one dealer said.
Apart from its normal quarterly statements and rare statements by the governor, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe does not traditionally comment on market views or speculation.
